concept.name: Delta
concept.definition: Delta is the first-order sensitivity of an option's price to a small change in the underlying's price: the partial derivative of option value with respect to the underlying price. A call delta ranges from 0 to +1 and a put delta from -1 to 0; the CFTC defines it as the expected change in an option's price per one-unit change in the underlying's price.
concept.intuition: Delta tells you how many shares of stock your option currently behaves like: a 0.50-delta call gains about fifty cents when the stock rises a dollar.
concept.mechanics: In Black-Scholes, call delta = N(d1) and put delta = N(d1) - 1 (for a non-dividend stock). Delta is the hedge ratio for delta-hedging, is used as a rough proxy for the risk-neutral probability of finishing in-the-money, and aggregates linearly across a portfolio. Delta itself changes as the underlying moves, which is what gamma measures.
concept.formula: Delta = dV/dS; Black-Scholes: call delta = N(d1), put delta = -N(-d1) = N(d1) - 1.
concept.failure_modes: Delta hedging is exact only for infinitesimal moves with all other inputs frozen; gaps, volatility changes, and time decay make realized hedge P&L diverge. The delta-as-probability proxy is only an approximation (it conflates N(d1) with the N(d2) exercise probability) and degrades for long-dated or high-volatility options.
concept.misconceptions: Delta is not the true real-world probability of finishing ITM — it is a sensitivity under the risk-neutral pricing framework. Nor is a delta-hedged position riskless: it remains exposed to gamma, vega, and theta.
concept.example: An XYZ $100 call with delta 0.60 gains roughly $0.60 when XYZ rises from $100 to $101; a trader long 10 such calls can delta-hedge by shorting 600 shares.

citations.source: CFTC Glossary — A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry
